## Overview

The Nambikwara, also called Nambikuára, Nambiquara, Alaketesu, or Anunsu, are an Indigenous people of Brazil who live in the Amazon, principally in Indigenous territories in Mato Grosso along the Guaporé and Juruena rivers. Currently about 1,150 Nambikwara live in these territories, whose villages are accessible from the Pan-American highway. Nambikwara is also the name of a Nambiquaran language spoken in Mato Grosso and neighbouring parts of Rondônia. The Nambikwara Nation is composed of many smaller bands, each with its own name. Their history includes early contact in 1770, the passage of Marechal Cândido Rondon through their territory, severe epidemics, the loss of territory to roads and farming companies, and extensive linguistic and anthropological documentation.

## Language & religion

Nambikwara is an indigenous language spoken by the Nambikwara in federal reserves covering approximately 50,000 square kilometres in Mato Grosso and neighbouring parts of Rondônia. UNESCO’s Atlas of the World Languages in Danger classifies it as vulnerable. The Nambikwara language family is divided into three major groups: Sabanê, Northern Nambikwara, also called Mamaindê, and Southern Nambikwara, also called Nambikwara.

Southern Nambikwara is a tonal language with three tones: a falling tone marked with a superscript “1,” a rising tone marked “2,” and a low tone marked “3.” Nambikwara is written in the Latin script. Its grammar includes main and subordinate verbs, indicative and imperative forms, seven kinds of pronouns, classifiers, tense, aspect, mood, voice, evidentiality, and an active-stative system for case marking. The language distinguishes remote past, mid past, recent past, present, and future, and marks sources of information through evidentiality.

Northern Nambikwara is spoken along the Roosevelt and Tenente Marques rivers and is divided into seven mutually intelligible dialects associated with the Da’wandê, Da’wendêm Âlpimentê, Yâlãkuntê, Yalakalorê, Mamaindê, and Negarotê people. Southern Nambikwara has four regional dialects, whose dialects are not mutually intelligible. The sources discuss missionaries, Christian education, Bible translation into Mamaindê, and learning Portuguese.
